I'm the kind of person who plays a game for the story, not the difficulty.  There's something that makes this game very special to me, and that's the Assist mode.  I suck at most video games--it took me 91 hours to beat Hollow Knight, and I only finished it because of the immortality mod I added to the game.  I turned on the Assist mode in Celeste, and not only beat the game, but had an incredible time doing so.

Another really awesome thing is the huge text in the game.  I'm visually impaired, and I almost started crying when I saw how big the font in this game is--I can actually read it, without having to use my magnification program, or smashing my face up against the screen.
I pirated Celeste at first but it was so good that I ended up buying it to support the creators and to have it in my steam favourites.

Due to the abundance of positive reviews, I couldn’t help but be drawn to [b]Celeste[/b]. Avoiding all spoilers, I strapped myself in for what many describe as a sublime experience.  Admittedly, I was a little let down in the beginning, as I had not yet understood the journey that awaited me. As I progressed and the story developed, I grew fonder of the game and ultimately felt pride in reaching the summit of Mount Celeste. The expression, “the journey is more important than the destination” fits this game to a T. 
Just a fair warning for those interested in the game: Celeste is a precision platformer and is often unforgiving, so be prepared to fail a lot (818 deaths during my first run).

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2176221722
[u][b]Played with PlayStation 4 controller[/b][/u]

[h1]✔️[u]Positive:[/u][/h1]
[b][+] Challenging is a very accurate description of the game.[/b]
Comparable to the likes of Super Meat Boy, Celeste is a 2D platformer that offers little room for mistakes - one hit kills you instantly and sends you back to the beginning of the screen. Thankfully, the respawn/reload times are very short, cushioning the player from the frustrations of frequent deaths. 

Deaths are (nearly) inevitable but given that the controls are simple and responsive, I never had the impression that the game was unfair; just difficult. Furthermore, each level introduces new platforming mechanics that gradually become more demanding as the level progresses. These nuances to your controls/movement add novelty and imbues progression with a sense of mastery. Definitely another great example of a game that is “easy to learn but difficult to master”.

[b][+] Diverse levels paired with sublime soundtracks.[/b]
This one is fairly straightforward, so I won’t go into too much detail. Every level has a unique theme, setting, and fantastic paired soundtrack. Check out the trailer for a quick taste. 

[b][+] The story is what sets Celeste apart from other games in this genre.[/b]
Yes, the gameplay is good but the story elevates this game to new heights [i](cause they climb a mountain, get it?)[/i]. While the story touches on many themes, mental health and personal growth are the centrepiece. It is clear that Madeline (the main character) suffers from a range of negative emotions (fear, anger, anxiety and depression), so much so that her emotions physically manifest in the form of Badeline (great name, I agree).

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2176221194
The progression of their relationship is nothing short of inspiring. [spoiler]What starts out as an antagonistic relationship, ends up being one of [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2177190353]partnership and encouragement.[/url][/spoiler] In scaling the mountain, Madeline shows incredible determination for self improvement. It is therefore immensely appropriate that the gameplay is challenging since the mountain is essentially a big metaphor for how frightening, discouraging, and challenging it can be to face your internal struggles. In fact, the journey was so touching that I felt encouraged to focus on my mental health.

[b][+] I especially loved the last level (Summit) as it combines the best of the story and gameplay.[/b]
In terms of gameplay, it serves as a challenging summary of your journey up the mountain by featuring the different platforming mechanics in a new setting. In terms of story, it marks the first big step to self improvement (physically represented by the summit) and the beginning of a great partnership between M(B)adeline. Overall just an excellent level.

[b][+] Completing the main story is only the tip of the iceberg.[/b]
The main game is not very long (~5 hours depending on your skill level) but is sufficiently challenging and long enough for plot development. The additional levels, however, are where things get really spicy. Hidden collectables in the form of crystal hearts and B-side cassettes unlock additional levels that are significantly harder than the main levels and were probably designed for precision platforming fanatics. I gave them an honest attempt but threw in the towel since I wasn’t enjoying myself. Regardless, it’s nice to have the option for harder levels, especially if you’re a masochist.

[h1]➖[u]Neutral:[/u][/h1]
[b][-] Celeste is a precision platformer, plain and simple.[/b]
It is clear that experiencing the difficulty of the game firsthand is central to the story/message but I would imagine that even the core game might be too challenging for most casual gamers. Despite having a great story that is alluring to many, it seems that the gameplay is intended for a niche audience. If you are unprepared, this could result in a frustrating experience rather than an elevating one.

[h1]❌[u]Negative:[/u][/h1]
[b][x] I experienced some technical difficulties concerning controller recognition:[/b] 
[1]When starting the game, if my first input is with the keyboard, I wouldn’t be able to get my controller to work. The only solution I found was to reset the game. 
[strike][2]Using the keyboard at all while playing (alt+tab or shift+tab, for example) often disconnects the controller. It would often take 30 seconds upon returning to the game for the controller to be functional again.[/strike]
Neither is a major cause for concern but a fix would be nice. 
 
[h1]🏅[u]Verdict:[/u][/h1]
[h1]★★★★✬ Excellent (if you enjoy precision platformers)[/h1]
Celeste is a fantastic experience but (likely) only if you fall within the niche of gamers that enjoy precision platformers. Even I, who typically loves platformers, sometimes found my patience wavering at times (nothing a little break couldn’t fix). However, it is vital to clarify that Celeste isn’t just about the platforming - it is the fusion of challenging gameplay and brilliant storytelling that sets this game apart. Failing is [u]required[/u] to fully immerse yourself in this heartwarming journey. 

Although I adore this game, I would only recommend this game if you are willing and ready to suffer (definitely worth it though).

I may not have panic attacks necessarily, but I've definitely had some anxiety problems for years. It feels like it's mostly under control now, but today something triggered it to flair up again. Normally I'd just keep fretting forever, but this game actually made me see my anxiety and some other aspects of myself in a different light, a kinder light. 

It's definitely a bit frustrating at points, but it's a challenge I know I can make easier at any point, but don't want to. Maybe, like the main character, I have something to prove, something to gain from the struggle. There's this moment of catharsis when I complete a tricky area and I find pride in collecting all the strawberries I can, even the tricky ones. The gameplay is excellent, and honestly? Normally I'd get frustrated by repeated deaths, but there's a moment where it essentially tells you it's okay to fail because you're learning from it, and that really just put a lot into perspective for me. 

The levels are gorgeous, the music is amazing, the sense of emotion is a little overwhelming at times, the gameplay is rewarding, and the characters and even the mountain itself flow seemlessly together into a good story and metaphor. 

As a gamer, a writer, a psychology student, and someone who's struggled with her own mental health, I have to say this game is excellent on all accounts. And if you're reading this, developers, thank you for all the kindness and care you put into this game. The experience might be legitimately life changing.

It took me ~12 hours to do so, while collecting 1/3 of all strawberries.  
I have played with a Controller, btw.

Speaking of strawberries - I really appreciate the game explicitly telling you that collecting them is only useful for bragging to your friends. It made it easier for me to justify skipping a lot of them and to just enjoy the game.

Overall, 10/10 game, I loved nearly every second of it.  
I can see why so many people play this game.  
I'll 100% think back to some lessons I've learned from this game in the future. We should all try to be more like Madeline.

So, overall: This game is a steal for 5€ on sale, check it out,

I don't play hard games.  I tried Dark Souls a few times, but kept getting dead by the big dude in the first room, or whatever.  I love games, have been playing them all my life - but I'm complete rubbish at them.

At first I dismissed Celeste along the lines of other super-hard pixelart platformers, but the reviews convinced me it was something worth experiencing.

So now I'm four worlds in, and loving it.  I'm even loving the challenge, and haven't bothered to use the assist mode once.  I'm happy to persist (and die hundreds of times each chapter) until I get it right.  The assist mode is a generous inclusion that I fully support, and I may yet use it.  The generous checkpointing also indicates, to me at least, that this is not a game that's hard for the sake of being hard - it's hard with the intent of building up your skills and rewarding your progress, not punishing your mistakes.

Worth the moneys.

Undoubtedly of the same quality as Super Meat Boy, VVVVVV, The End is Nigh, N++, etc.

A must-play for 2D platformers lovers.

It is not difficult to imagine that Celeste, perhaps the most well-received platformer game, ticks all the boxes: pretty pixel art, great soundtrack, simple and tight controls, and most importantly, excellent level design.

But that is not all about Celeste. IMHO, what makes Celeste particularly shine is how it has both breadth and depth while welcoming all kinds of players, from casual gamers to die-hard fans of precision platformers, and even to speedrunners. If you are intrigued to know how this feat is accomplished, read the following paragraphs with asterisk, which are mostly spoiler-free resumé of Celeste's content. Otherwise, feel free to skip to the end of this review.

Celeste has 8 chapters, each has an A-side, a B-side, and a C-side (a reference to records and cassettes), and a Farewell chapter.

* Each A-side chapter has its unique visual style and soundtrack, and introduces new interactable objects. Playing through the A-sides gives you a full taste of the story and mechanics of Celeste. The main story, which is about [spoiler]facing your depression and embracing your inner self[/spoiler] and is inspired by the true emotional experience of the main dev themselves during the development, spans from chapter 1-A to 7-A. So technically, the more difficult 8-A can be skipped by the most causal players. Collectibles [spoiler](strawberries, cassettes which unlock B-sides, crystal hearts which unlock the main area of chapter 8 and Farewell)[/spoiler] are completely optional and can be safely skipped. They are often hidden or situated in more difficult paths, and tease those who want a little more challenge for their upward journey.

* If you don't aim for those collectibles, the difficulty of the A-sides is gentle and manageable even for platformer newbies. There are checkpoints on almost every screen. When you die, you respawn at the checkpoint of the same room, typically from a couple of seconds ago. Hence, the penalty of dying is minimal. The game even encourages you to be proud of your death counts, which are the witness of your perseverance and progress. As a precision platformer, there is no doubt Celeste won't be easy for everyone. But Celeste is considerate enough to include an in-game assist mode that allows you to change game speed (down to 50%), to add invincibility, or to have infinite stamina or dashes, etc. You see, Celeste really gives you carte blanche to play the game in your own way, and it only wants you to enjoy your climbing.

* B-sides, with roughly half the number of rooms compared to their corresponding A-sides, introduce no new mechanics. They are like a condensed and more difficult counterpart of their A-sides: no story, no cutscene, no collectible, just Madeline and intense platforming levels, curated for fans of precision platformer.

* C-sides, unlocked by completing all B-sides, have few rooms but very lengthy ones, unlike most rooms in A-sides and B-sides. Here, your skills and consistency are tested to the highest standard so far.

* The Farewell chapter, also known as chapter 9, is the ultimate conclusion of Madeline's journey at Celeste Mountain. This lengthy chapter introduces new mechanics and is filled with rooms of difficulty parallel to those in B-sides and C-sides.

* For the most intrepid souls, completing all the aforementioned chapters is not even close to the end of the challenge: there are collectibles [spoiler](golden strawberries)[/spoiler] awarded for completing a chapter without dying once.

* Speedrunners would be euphoric to learn that Celeste's levels are designed with speedrunning in mind. More concretely, there are many hidden moves and techniques. As a matter of fact, these advanced moves are under your sleeve from the very beginning, you just don't know it yet. They are not necessary for most players, since learning those few moves taught in the game suffices to complete the game. However, mastering these moves allows you to traverse rooms much faster by taking unconventional paths. These paths, a brilliant demonstration of the excellent level design, are intentionally left in the rooms for the most skilful players; they appear to be downright impossible without knowing advanced techniques, so that beginners won't even consider them as a possibility and spend time trying in vain.

As an average player, it took me more than 50 hours and a grand total of over 20,000 deaths to complete all the chapters: a dozen hours for the A-sides and collectibles, a dozen more hours for the B-sides, a dozen more for the C-sides, and a final dozen for the Farewell chapter. What amazes me most during these hours is that many times when I first look at a playthrough video, a room appears to be fiendishly difficult, and I doubt I could ever make it. However, it turns out, every single time, that with enough patience and practice, I can really pull it off, and even consistently.

Climbing is not easy. Nor is this precision platformer with a climbing setting. Playing through those difficult rooms, deaths after deaths and occasionally stuck for hours, sometimes feels more like enduring and persevering than having fun. But it feels so good when I advance little by little in the same room, until I finally perform consistently enough to make it through. And those deaths and struggles become commemorable when I finally complete a whole chapter, which always makes me jubilant as if I reached the summit of a real mountain. In that sense, I find the climbing setting of Celeste surprisingly appropriate. Persevere, then triumph. This maxim taught by Celeste also applies to our life, doesn't it?

A huge, beautiful, brutal platformer with blinding polish and a difference in philosophy:  it wants you to beat everything it's got, because [i]you[/i] can do anything.  That's what the story's about, that's what the game itself is about -- channeling all the fractured, doubting parts of oneself, compressing the dissociated, gaseous will into a beam of hot plasma that can burn through the barrier of the impossible and open a tunnel to the golden land of victory.  [i]Celeste[/i]'s message is empowerment through sweat, and the change that comes over us when we embrace, rather than evade, the difficulties of life.

This is a game that's worth hundred-percenting.  I did it without ever activating assist mode, and though I died nearly 9,000 times, I never once felt I couldn't conquer an obstacle.  Even a string of 500 deaths in a row could not shake my confidence and drop me into a rut of nervous failure, and I owe that to the game's uniquely uplifting atmosphere.  It would not surprise me if playing [i]Celeste[/i] pulled some people out of depression.  

If you play 2D action games at all, this is an essential addition to your Steam library.   

(Changing Madeline's hair color to show how many midair dashes she has left is a brilliant idea!  And have you ever played a game that doesn't teach you how to perform some powerful techniques until the end?  They were so simple, I'm surprised I didn't pull them off by accident earlier!  Ingenious!)

This game is incredible. Not only is it one of the best precision platformers out there, it also has a very creative and poignant story focusing on the main character's depression and her attempts to grapple with it. 

[i]Celeste[/i] does so many things well that it almost feels blasphemous to criticize it (but I'll try!). 

The good:

-The story. Our main character, Madeline, is "stuck in a cycle." She's full of self-doubt, plagued by trauma, and suffers from panic attacks and depression. She is determined to accomplish a very difficult task: reaching the summit of Celeste Mountain. Along the way, we encounter interesting characters such as Badeline (a "Part of You") -- the physical manifestation of Madeline's pessimism, restraint, anger, risk-aversion, fear, and insecurity. Do you try to detach or silence this part of yourself that is constantly keeping you down, or do you learn how to live with it instead and possibly grow stronger? There were a number of cutscenes in this game with some really moving lines that left me feeling a little teary-eyed. I found it to be a very relatable story, and I loved the direction they went with it.

-The graphics. The artwork is great - there's a variety of level designs that are popping with color and contrast, and every stage is a pleasure to look at. Color is used very effectively in the game mechanics as well, such as the shade of Madeline's hair indicating how many jumps/dashes are remaining.

-The music. The OST is just so good. Even when you are dying repeatedly and feeling frustrated, somehow it's more palatable because you've got a kickass level theme in the background. Harder variants of the same level also offer remixed tracks, which is a great way to spice things up. Lots of memorable bops in this one.

-The controls. These are buttery-smooth and super responsive. You have a great deal of control over your character, whether you're scaling structures, hopping from wall to wall, or making a descent. The one critique I have here - which may be more attributable to my own shortcomings or controller issues - is that the analog joystick made navigation/handling a lot riskier due to occasional misdirects between axis-aligned actions and diagonal ones. I found that the D-pad and keyboard were much better alternatives.

-The difficulty. There's something for everyone, whether you're a total novice or an ultra-hardcore type. If you're normally intimidated by platforming games, there is an Assist Mode that lets you do things like skip levels, grant yourself invulnerability, slow down the game speed, etc. If you ever get stuck on a certain section or just aren't a fan of the level, you can always force your way past it and enjoy the rest of the game. There are also strawberries and hidden crystal hearts you can collect in each stage, which gives you plenty of incentive to explore and seek out additional challenges. The standard game has 8 chapters, defaulting to the easiest versions of each level -- they're still tough on their own merits, but if you want a greater challenge, there are harder versions of these levels that you can unlock, as well as a difficult DLC level (Chapter 9: Farewell). And if you want even more than that, you can get into things like speedruns, no-death runs, or mods/custom maps from the very active Celeste community (the 2020 Spring Community Collab is a lot of fun). In short, while the base game does present a challenge by default, this game is ultimately as easy or as hard as you want it to be.

The so-so:

-As much as I love the gameplay and difficulty of this game, some parts do feel a little [i]too[/i] frustrating when playing casually the first time through, where you die again and again and again until you happen to execute the correct move on the correct area of pixels. It can sometimes feel more like succeeding from luck rather than skill. However, upon returning to these sections during a second playthrough after having gained more experience, they were miraculously super-easy and I almost wondered what had given me so much trouble the first time around. So while I do think everything in the game is "fair" and can be handled with enough skill, some tasks are (in my opinion) a little out of place and should be moved later in the game.

-I wish Madeline's stamina status came with a bar indicator or something. During some particularly tough platforming sections, I'd be unsure how much stamina I had left until it was too late. 

The bad:

-Those janky core blocks in Chapter 8 are brutal. Just yeet those suckers out of the game. They're simply not enjoyable - they're very analog, and require so much precision and timing to wrangle properly. Even after 100%'ing this game, I still suck at handling them with any real sense of control. 

Conclusion:

At $20, this game is a killer deal. If you enjoy precision platforming in any capacity, this game is among the best. Definitely check this one out.

Celeste is my favorite game of all time, bar none, and it has been since I first played it six years ago on my Switch. Even after hundreds of hours of playing this game, I can see myself playing this game for hundreds of hours more without tiring of it. Its story, art style, music, and gameplay make it an experience that is hard to forget.

STORY

Celeste's story is probably its most captivating aspect on a first playthrough. Though it doesn't necessarily have most complex narrative, Celeste's characters are well-written and memorable, and its emotional moments are deeply moving, despite the story's simplicity. My favorite part of the story is that instead of simply existing alongside the visuals, music, and gameplay, it is accentuated by these other aspects of the game more so than I find many other games' stories to be.

VISUALS

People often talk about pixellated graphics in games as if they are inherently inferior to games with more realistic graphics. I find Celeste to be a compelling case against this viewpoint, as its visuals make the game look absolutely stunning at some points, despite its "low quality" graphics. Specifically, the color palettes used in each section often complement the mood of that section of the story very well. There are also the cartoon-style portraits representing each character during dialogue - though they might at first seem to clash with the game's pixel graphics during gameplay, I find that these portraits create a nice contrast in art style that make the game look more vibrant. And that's not even to mention the beautiful 3-D modeled mountain that occupies the background in the game's overworld map and title screen.

MUSIC

It's undeniable Celeste's soundtrack was Lena Raine's big break onto the music scene, and it surely doesn't disappoint. Celeste has one of the best and most memorable soundtracks I've ever heard in a game, and both its soft moments and bursts of energy accentuate the story and gameplay perfectly. It's not hard to see why, after Celeste, several other games, most notably Minecraft, enlisted Lena's help on their soundtracks. Though it would also be remiss of me not to mention Lena's fantastic solo work, my favorite of which has to be the EP "Singularity" released under the pseudonym of "Kuraine."

GAMEPLAY

As important as the previous categories are, to me, by far the most important place for a game to succeed is in its gameplay. And, to me, this is where Celeste shines brightest. It should be extremely apparent to anyone who has played this game for any serious length of time that the developers put a lot of care into the way movement feels in this game. Whenever you fail in Celeste, you have no one to blame but yourself, and, for a game as brutal as Celeste can be, that is extremely important. I am constantly impressed by how nuanced this game's movement is, and how it so seamlessly caters both to beginners still just grasping the controls and experts with hundreds or even thousands of hours.

DIFFICULTY

It's no secret that Celeste is a difficult game. Heck, "Difficult" is literally the second tag on its Steam page, right behind "Precision Platformer." Undoubtedly, a game as difficult as Celeste would be hard to stomach if its movement was any less refined than it is. And it's surely by no mistake that Celeste has such consistently stellar level design to accommodate this difficulty. But also, a story about overcoming obstacles as moving as Celeste's would be hard to tell without the player having to go through the same difficulties, frustrations, and setbacks as Madeline. That's where the true beauty of this game's story comes into play, is in its difficulty.

ASSIST MODE

On release, Celeste was lauded for its "Assist Mode," which allows players to adjust the games difficulty if they find the game to be too challenging to overcome but still ultimately want to engage with the games story. And this "Assist Mode" surely holds a lot of nuance, too, allowing players a lot of room for adjustment, ranging from just slowing the game down a little bit to fully making Madeline invincible. Personally, I can't say I'm a big fan of this mode. While I'm normally all for making games accessible to as many people as possible, with a game like Celeste, where the story is so inextricably tied to the game's difficulty, removing the difficulty can make the story feel cheapened as a result. Not to mention the fact that turning off Assist Mode removes the stamp that indicates you've used Assist Mode, which is a weird decision that can make it difficult to verify the legitimacy of achievements in the game, though that may be a moot point.

MODDING

While I normally wouldn't consider a game's modding community when reviewing it, with a community as vibrant as Celeste's it wouldn't be right not to bring up. Celeste has one of the easiest modloaders to both install and use of any game I've played, being surpassed only by Terraria's Steam integration with Tmodloader. There are also modded maps of a wide range of difficulties, ranging from "Beginner" all the way to "Grandmaster," so even if you've only beaten the main game and don't plan to tackle anything more difficult, there is probably still something that will appeal to you in modded Celeste.

CONCLUSION

This game is good. Like, really good. I personally think it's worth picking up at its $20 price point, but even if you aren't willing to pay that much, it frequently goes on sale for as little as $5, so there's really no reason not to give it a go. Perfection. Best 2D platformer of the decade and for me best of all time. Celeste is a game about challenge, the challenge the protagonist Madeline faces in the form of her anxiety, pessimism, and sheer lack of confidence as she attempts to climb Celeste mountain. The challenge for the player is to tackle and triumph these mastercrafted levels that will test your platforming to its limits. However this isn't to say Celeste is inaccessible to people new to platforming, the game teaches you beautifully how to control Madeline by constructing levels that scale incredibly well difficulty wise. Celeste like all great games aids the player in polishing their skill set through the level design. By the end of every level you'll feel as though you have mastered the latest mechanic introduced to you while also feeling like a more precise and quick witted version of yourself. 

This game is the whole package. The story and characters make you want to climb the mountain, the internal conflict Madeline experiences is a struggle not uncommon with young adults. But persevering through, and finding your way to the top of that mountain is what makes Celeste such an uplifting masterpiece of a game. 

Prepare to play a real game, and keep your head up. This game is challenging but it is also very rewarding, this experience was designed meticulously with so much love and care that you could sink several dozens of hours into finding every corner new content is hiding in. A must buy and an absolute masterpiece, do yourself a favour and pickup Celeste.

Celeste, one of the greatest games ever made. And here is why. Firstly, let me point out that I have played a lot of this game. I mostly play mods nowadays, but I'm currently grinding doing all the levels deathless. This review will be mostly spoiler free, but a few level mechanics will be brought up.

MECHANICS

Celeste is a relatively simply platforming game at first glance, until you take a closer look. You have a few abilities at your disposal. You have your basic jump and walk, you can climb walls and jump between them, and you have a dash, which can be used on the ground or in the air. SImple, right? But one of the things that makes this game great is that the developers know what the people want. And what the people want is speed. There is NO speed cap in Celeste. Nada. Zilch. And there are many ways to build up speed. So you can get going really fast. Now I couls spend a lot of time talking about the different tech you can do, such as a reverse extended hyperdash bunnyhop into a double block boosted chained ultra. (Which is tech only used in the hardest of the hard mods.) But that stuff can be learned on your own time. 

STORY

Hooo, Boi. Celeste has got one heck of a story. I'll keep this spoiler free, but simply put, it is the story of someone climbing a literal mountain while struggling with a mental mountain at the same time. Madeline, our protagonist, sets out to climb a mountain to show that she can do anythings. But the mountain isn't any ordinary mountain. It brings out the worst in people. So while climbing she has to deal with her internal turmoil being physically manifested around her. And, I could be wrong on this, I'm pretty sure its also a personal story about the developer.

LEVEL DESIGN

Celeste has some really briliiant mechanics in each level, and all the levels are quite pretty. Besides your relatively generic platformer mechanics, such as wind or ice, there are also some really unique ones, like blocks that move when you dash, or my personal favorite, Kevin. Kevins, whenever you hit them move towards the direction you hit them from. You hit them on their right side, they move right. But they look hilarious. And some of the secrets are really well hidden. Too be completely honest, I did use a walkthrough in my first playthrough, but only for the stuff I missed, which waas a lot. There are even a handful of puzzle secrets.

DEVELOPERS

Celeste has some of the best developers of any game I have seen. Period. They listen to their community, and react based on that. For some examples, when the Farewell Update came a while back, the developers added a few things to cater to players and the community. Firstly, in the new level they added, there were a few really secret rooms that showed off some speedrun tech that had been discovered which wasn't intentional. There is a whole puzzle hidden in farewell that, when completed, will reveal some of the biggest names on the Celeste community. And lastly, my favorite, is the secret Kevin save. (I like Kevins, OK?) A few years back, there was a TAS that was made for Celeste. (For those who don't know, a TAS is basically a player playing the game one frame at a time.) The TASsers had changed the Kevins to make a noise that sounded like, Fwuhuhu, or Fwahaha. The developers found this hilarious, so when they updated the game, they added a hidden save name that would make them say this noise. For those who are curious, the save name is FWAHAHA.

MODS

If you have finished this game and are hungry for more, then let me tell you, there is a ton of mods to play. And they can get a lot harder then your regular old Celeste. I would highly recommend, if you are starting to mod to get the Strawberry Jam Mod, Speedrun Tool, and Monika's D Sides. Monika's D sides are a pretty hard  mod, harder than any part of regular Celeste, and really fun. Speedrun Tool is a almost essential tool that lets you make savestates. This is helpful for longer rooms when you need to practice the end bit. And finally, Strawberry Jam. This mod is MASSIVE. There are over 100 levels, 100+ custom songs, was worked on by 300+ developers, and offers a wide range of difficulty, from beginner to advanced to Grandmaster to GM+1.

OTHER CRITIQUES I HAVE SEEN OF THIS GAME

Lastly, I feel that it is necessary to discuss the negative reviews that I have seen. There are two common complaint: Accessibility and Difficulty. Firstly, accessibilty. There is some fair complaint in here. One, there is no colorblind mode. Now, I am color blind myself, (Yellows and Greens, Blues and Purples.) but I didn't have any trouble. However, it is quite possible that it could impede you playing the level, especially for darker ones like chapter 5. There is also one color based puzzle in the game, which can be trouble some when colorblind. Second, the keyboard controls. This game was  rather noticably designed for controller. This is really obvious in the feather mechanic. In chapter 6, you get accsess to a feather which will give you flight and 360 degree movement for a short time. This, when starting out, can be really hard to work on keyboard. HOWEVER. I would highly recommend playing on keyboard for one simple reason. Diagonal dashes. (For note here, I have fully beaten the game on both an Xbox and my PC.) Digonals are really hard to do on controlller, and will often send you right or up instead. And in the last chapter of the game it teaches you a tech called wavedashes. Wavedashes are a movement technique where you dash diagonally down into the ground and then jump. This gives you a big speed boost and is a required part of Farewell. This. was. TORTURE. on controller. (As a sidenote, I saw one reviewer complaining about the inconsistency of the tech, and I can tell you that with a bit of practice, it it extrememly consistent. After I finished Farewell on PC, I almost never failed it again.) If you enjoy this game and are/eill be considering modding it, you want keyboard. Precision is the name of the game, and controllers just don't bring that too the table. Other then this accesssibility issues, the game is pretty good at working for all types of players, and even has an assist mode if you find the game to be too hard.

Which brings us to the second complaint: DIfficulty. Don't get me wrong, Celeste is a really hard game. And you are going to die a lot. I died probably 20k times on my first playthrough, and have probabl died 200k+ times now. But it is not absurdly/ Kaizo level hard. And if you are struggling, use assist mode. Its ok to use it. Its what its there for.


CONCLUSION

This was a rather long review, so I'll take my leave now, hoping that I convinced somebody to play this masterpiece. It wil be hard, and sometime it will feel like you are not making any progress and keep falling down to the bottom of the mountain. [h1] Introduction [/h1]
Celeste is a platformer game that has some rogue-like air about it. The game is simple to learn, and it introduces the player to mechanics as they keep playing them. Keeping things interesting while gradually raising the difficulty, it makes for one of the best games in this genre and a game that has almost literally no flaws. Every element has been taken care of with the utmost cared (save for a few minor details) and it addresses the difficulty innovatively.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
The gameplay is that of a platformer but with a good amount of twist to it. You control Madeline and must go through levels to advance to reach the end goal, the mountain. In levels, you can expect to climb-jump of walls, dash to reach long distances, solve puzzles, deal with hazardous danger, explore secrets and discover more about its mechanics.

One of the things Celeste does very well is to address the barrier that comes to the player in the form of difficulty. Sometimes players don't get into games because if it is too hard, is not fun and if you cheat, is boring. This is done thanks to assisting mode, which makes it so that the player can control some aspects of the game without making them feel particularly bad. This serves as training wheels so that the player can depend on them until they can beat levels without it.

Rather than cutting off mechanics or other elements of the game, assist mode gives advantages of the type such as more dashes, being invincible, stopping time to calculate your direction before a dash and other stuff. The developer wants people to finish the game feeling good, that they accomplished something and to enjoy its overall message of not giving up. That is not to say that the assist mode is bad. It is something to rely on should you need it, no one starts being a master and everyone is different.

[h1] Be proud of your death count, it shows how much you've learned![/h1]

As for the levels themselves, they are each colorful bit that works like an intricated maze. There are secret rooms with collectibles to discover and a lot of well, platforming. Celeste makes the game simple enough at first, but the last levels will require a good degree of skill. In this design that follows a mountain-like shape of getting harsher to climb every time, it presents players with a challenge. To see who good they can get at the game and enjoy the learning experience.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2012992053

The player can expect to die quite a lot in this game, however, the deaths itself are not too punishing. Respawning them at checkpoints and allowing them another try without interrupting gameplay. There are various elements, from lava to shadows that appear when you last touched a platform or winds that can push you back. These elements will add something of a unique approach to their corresponding levels and change how the player moves through them.

The controls are simple and have no lag in the action, giving you full control of Madeline. Often you might think about how to approach a situation before jumping it or reacting to unexpected elements. While the game itself doesn't present bosses in the traditional senses, some segments are confrontations and involve beating other characters. These are a joy to play as they have their way of being deal with and make up for moments of high precision and reaction.

[h1] Story [/h1]
The story in Celeste is pretty and nice. It entails Madeline wanting to climb this mountain and working towards that goal. Dealing with elements such as self-doubt, but also of not giving up and facing challenges up ahead. The cast is colorful, and their voices are made in the style of games like Banjo-Kazooie, with sounds. This makes for a more vibrant and delightful experience of the story. To witness the full story, players will have to beat mirror levels and collect all hearts. I recommend players to go for this on the second run of levels, and simply have fun during their first time.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2012993091

[h1] What Makes It Special [/h1]
What makes Celeste special is that all its elements are impeccable, from it's gameplay to the visual or overall story. The sound design is excellent, featuring a good number of tracks to listen to during the levels while it's visuals are beautiful pixel art that has been done with a lot of care. I would say that Celeste can be an artistic game just because of how well these aspects have done in representing the game despite the focus being its message and gameplay.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2012990647

It is also special because of assist mode. The game is challenging and can become a huge wall at times, but there is no shame in needing help. The developers recommend you play it without assist mode during your first run (as the mirrors levels and last segments can become gruesome) but they understand that all players are different. This is wonderful because the player doesn't have to fear the possibility of getting stuck or frustrated if they cannot beat a level. It also allows the player to discover the trajectory they could probably take when playing the level without assist mode.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
Celeste is one of the best games in this genre out there and that is not an exaggeration. It is a game that is hard for me to find flaws in it and that I thoroughly enjoyed. This is a must-buy for sure if you like these types of games and if you are not a fan of difficult games or platformers, you should still consider adding it to your collection. It is a very special and unique experience that most certainly you would enjoy. Its price on sale is an absolute steal and is among the most wonderful titles I had played ever.

Through and through, everything the developers of Celeste set out to accomplish came to fruition in full. Every last part of this game feels realized to its fullest potential, and with even more content coming in early 2019 as a free "farewell" to Celeste, there's absolutely no reason as to why anyone shouldn't play it.

At a mechanical level Celeste is outwardly a very straightforward, no-frills game. You can jump, wall-jump, dash in the air and climb. That's it, at a glance at least. The way that these mechanics come together and come to have their potential maximized is through different, mostly chapter-specific "gimmicks" for lack of a better word. Whether it's through resetting your air dash's cooldown through hitting a gem or having your moveset affect the environment in different ways, the game constantly keeps itself fresh. Each one of these gimmicks starts simply and is utilized more creatively as you become more used to them, leading to a natural progression of difficulty in each chapter that is handled incredibly fairly while still remaining somewhat difficult, but difficulty is something that will be touched upon later as it goes far beyond the main game itself.

The story, without going into much detail delves into personal struggle with Celeste mountain being synonymous with the main character Madeline's own personal mountain that she must overcome. While depression and anxiety are brought up quite frequently in games nowadays to the point where it could be considered pretty trope-y, Celeste handles it in an incredibly fresh way that makes it feel incredibly genuine and touching. The game's worth it for the narrative alone, in my opinion and worth playing even if you couldn't care less about the story.

Visually, not much needs to be said as it's pretty apparent from screenshots or a bit of video of the game. It's stunning and stands out in both a genre and an artstyle that has been oversaturated over the years. There's a level of polish and care that Celeste has that just isn't there in a vast majority of other games, and that extends far beyond its art. The music largely follows suit and is complimentary to the game with a few stand-out tracks that speak volumes as to the potential of Lena Raine(Kuraine) and the various artists who did remixes for the B-Sides of the game's chapters.

Where Celeste truly shines, though, is in the way that its deeper levels of difficulty are handled. Through exploring the chapters in the main game, there's various different collectibles: strawberries, crystal hearts and cassettes are the main three. While strawberries are often gated behind each chapter's harder, optional stages, they ultimately serve no purpose aside from the satisfaction of acquiring them/completing them all. Crystal hearts are often gated behind puzzles which don't make themselves readily apparent as you play, but once you stumble upon your first one, you'll begin to look at everything in a way that makes them more easily noticed. They serve as a means to gate the game's "true ending" until you've fully explored the main game's chapters.

The cassettes, however, are usually found on a hidden side path in each chapter. They unlock B-Sides which are an alternate, harder version of the chapter that they are found in. They push each chapter's gimmicks incredibly closely to their limit and are your source of post-game content in Celeste. Each B-Side is accompanied by a remixed version of the original track found in each chapter which are phenomenal across the board. In early 2019, as recently announced, stages that are even more difficult are going to be added as the game's final farewell. 

Personally, Celeste is my game of the year 2018 and one of my favorite games of all time. It's the type of game that has something for everyone and I genuinely believe that it's an experience not to be missed.

The story of [b]Celeste[/b] starts out with [b]Madeline[/b], who goes to [b]Mount Celeste[/b] with the goal of climbing to the top. An [b]Old Woman[/b] tells [b]Madeline[/b] that climbing [b]Mount Celeste[/b] is a foolish idea and that she should turn back but [b]Madeline[/b] refuses and presses on.

[b]Celeste[/b] is a 2D platformer that is very simple but has some challenging gameplay tied to it. You will die, a lot, and you will die in one hit, so be careful, although you can use that death as a learning experience. I honestly liked the challenge that [b]Celeste[/b] provided and it did feel fair for someone who has played a bunch of 2D platformers.

TL;DR: This game isn't just about difficult platforming, although it is marketed and popularized as such.

Long version: This is one of the few games I paid full price for soon after release, and I don't regret it. It's a game about overcoming personal challenges, both in gameplay and in story. The difficulty of the game lies not in imprecise controls, like with Human Fall Flat, but with varied and interesting level design. In most games, deaths feel like failure and are portrayed as negative, with Game Over screens and perhaps some blood and gore, or maybe a bit of waiting around for things in the level to move into place. This game treats death differently. The animation for dying is quick, and you respawn quickly. Moving elements in the level are reset so you can immediately start moving again, without having to wait for things to line up. The music in the background doesn't reset, which is important for feeling a sense of continuity. Frequent checkpoints make death less painful, and death becomes an opportunity to practice platforming skills rather than a punishment for sub-par gameplay.

Story-wise, the player character deals with depression, anxiety, panic attacks, and low self-esteem. A character she meets on her way up the mountain copes with the passing on of a loved one and the search for a meaning in existence. Yet another character faces... faces a sort of kodokushi, and the bittersweet feeling of seeing a treasured thing fade from its former glory. He's hard for me to describe, but he is no less realistic than any other character. They all have unique situations that they need to personally handle, and the writing recognizes that. I like this game because it does that, and does it well. Entire chapters or sequences of them are themed around these characters, with their own color palettes, sound design, music, level design, and game mechanics.

If the platforming itself is too difficult, as it likely is for many potential buyers, you can go into Assist Mode and change the game speed, number of air dashes, or invincibility. This changes the game from a difficult platformer to an exploration game, but doesn't trivialize gameplay or level design. Despite the fact that death can be rendered impotent, there are still puzzles that need to be solved in order to progress through a level, switches that must be pressed and collectibles to be found. That is my favorite part of this game; even when one of the central mechanics is removed, this game is still enjoyable. This game can fit into two genres, that of difficult platforming and of leisurely exploration. This duality mirrors the physical and mental representations of the mountain that the characters face in the story, and makes the game accessible for more casual or less able players. This game isn't just about difficult platforming, and I commend it for that.

Thank you for reading my review, and I welcome any criticisms or comments you may have.

MY EXPERIENCE 

I'd heard that this was a platformer game about depression when I was around 12-13 years old. I somehow, with my inexperienced gamer hands, managed to struggle through the game and reach the top of the mountain. I thought the game was a cute indie game with AMAZING graphics, amazing music, and pretty charming characters. Didn't seem that deep, but I thought it was cool that the game was about depression, even if I didn't quite see it.


I'm much older now. I'm wiser now. I've gone to therapy, I've taken medication, and I've had to do a lot of soul searching.

Then, I bought the game (on my laptop this time) on a whim, and Madeline and I started climbing up the mountain. I was not ready for how many emotions this game would make me feel.

Climbing up that mountain means so much more to me now, because that's how I felt. Back when I first played it, I was like Madeline. I was struggling and fighting, but only half knowledgeable on what I was fighting for. Back then, I didn't realize that fighting through my struggles in life would be difficult and painful ("You might see things. Things you ain't ready to see."), I just thought it would heal me. Back then, I didn't realize that the bad and ugly parts of me were parts of me I had to learn to live with and *heal*.

When I replay this game, I'm feeling all the things I felt back then and realizing, "Oh. I wasn't alone. I couldn't have known better." Now, when I play as Madeline, I feel like I'm helping her climb the mountain that I climbed. Every inch of this game just oozes with meaning, and kindness, and experience, you just have to feel for it. Sometimes, you don't know you're climbing the mountain to find yourself. Sometimes, you don't know climbing that mountain will change your life. Sometimes you just think you're climbing the mountain.

These characters are designed around mental health in a way that's hard to articulate. Sure, you can say Madeline is panic disorder, the mountain is depression, Oshiro is OCD, but they're all so much more than that. Like humans, they aren't just labels decorated in a certain way to make it fit. 

This isn't a depressing game like I expected when I heard it was about mental health, and that just makes it all that much better. Celeste is charming, and it's hopeful! It's about just how rewarding it is to push through the difficulties and learn to work with yourself rather than against yourself. It's about how there's always sunshine at the top of the mountain, and that you aren't alone while climbing it.


PERSONAL STORIES OVER

Okay, the gameplay really is impeccable. The controls are easy to understand and intuitive, but the mechanics allow for complexity where necessary. There's a good challenge, but the accessible Assist Mode makes it so this game really is for everyone. The art is STUNNING, with the backgrounds being some of the prettiest I've ever seen and the character portraits being charming.

DO I RECOMMEND THIS GAME?

Yes. I recommend this game. If you're a "bad" gamer- good news, you can learn. If you can't learn, you can get assistance, and there's no shame in it. If you're a hardcore gamer, you've found your place- the community here is unreal. If you're struggling with finding yourself, this game welcomes you with open arms.

I. Some stupid pre-history
The reason I started playing this game was my inability to handle with frequent deaths in games. Usually if I die twice or thrice while playing some tough game I go into a rage and close that game, abandoning it for months. I decided to get rid of that Part of Me. So I bought Celeste and promised myself to complete its main story at all costs. (then i changed my mind and set a higher goal to complete all B-Sides) UPD1: I'VE COMPLETED ALL THE C-SIDES!!!
UPD2: I'VE COMPLETED THE WHOLE GAME FULLY!

II. Difficulty
What I found really helpful and interesting in Celeste is that it can fit anyone's wishes. From those people, who have never played platformers and are not really strong-willed to suffer a lot, to people who can spend days completing one super-hard level - everyone will find their difficulty.
I divide it like that:
1. Assist Mode - easy
2. A-Sides - normal
3. B-Sides - hard
4. C-Sides and Farewell - extremely hard
5. Speedruns/Golden Strawberry runs - AI

III. Graphics
You know, I did really enjoy graphics here. I have never expected pixel-graphics can appear that beatiful. Sometimes backgrounds can be so magnificent that it takes breath. Also there're some CG's which will appear while completing storyline. They look nice and you feel like artist put his heart into it.

IV. Audio
Lena Raine, the composer of Celeste soundtrack, did an incredible job there. Music in Celeste will always help you not to get angry and keep on playing. Moreover, some compositions that play in some story-important moments, can fit atmosphere perfectly and emphasize emothions you get from game. After finishing Celeste, I even downloaded some tracks and I sometimes listen to it.

V. Gameplay
I can't say what is innovative about it or something because as I've already said, that's my first platformer game. But I really enjoyed it. Celeste has a wide range of movements, some of which can stay unrevealed even after completing the game, a lot of objects with unique behaviour, and something I was really amazed to see - some chapters introduce us the wind mechanic. Wind will take you to the side it blows to. So I never got bored while playing. Each chapter introduces something new and interesting.

VI. Story
There're some people who say there's nothing about it, but most of them doesn't think like that. As for me, the storyline is really inspiring. It tells us about a girl called Madeline, living in depression and anxiety, who came to the Celeste Mountain to fight against herself and climb to the summit. While playing, you will get to know a lot about her before climbing the mountain, about her character. Also few characters will be introduced to the player, each of them is important for the story. Audio, graphics and story, working together, do a perfect job and make you understand why Madeline is climbing this mountain and you sympathize here a lot. This game can make you more persistent and self-confident and it can help you to climb your own life mountain.

I think everyone should play Celeste. Thanks to its difficulty system no one will stay dissatisfied. Thanks for reading!

SPOILERS AHEAD

Celeste is just like programming, and here's why.

You start off slow. Hello world? Jump-dash? For gods sake, I thought this was supposed to be hard.

A few levels later and oh shit, they weren't kidding. 

Your failures will be many, and will come fast. You stop even thinking of them as failures and as part of the game itself. The mistakes will be of either the "I'm a moron" or the "WHY DIDN'T THAT WORK???" varieties. You die slightly later in the level, your error comes a little farther down the program, and even that failure carries a sense of accomplishment. Every single iteration, you get closer, gain more skills. 

Eventually you're jumping and dodging with lightning-fast reflexes that you never thought you would have. You beat the level, your program runs, you bask in your glory for a moment, then immediately go on to the next one -- another behemoth of a challenge to overcome. A mix of excitement and dread. But you did it before, and you'll do it again.

Eventually once things get tougher you go online and watch tutorials, even though it feels like cheating, but every time you do, it makes you smarter than you were before. You see the experts doing way better than you think you'll ever do. How do you even begin to write an app like that, or scale the mountain in 45 minutes? There's no possible way to beat that B-Side, are you kidding me?? 

Sometimes it'll get so frustrating you'll put it down for days. But you always come back, because the challenge is still there, sitting on your computer, waiting for you to overcome. 

Then, hours and hours later, you look back on Forsaken City, just play it again to see how much better you've gotten. Through no formal training, no tutorials, no guidance except maybe reading the forums, you've gotten ten times better, just through trying, failing, and trying again.

This is the only Steam review I've ever written. Thanks for reading.

There's no beating around the bush, Celeste is one of the best 2D platformers I've had the pleasure of playing in a long time. It's initially quite unassuming, since you think to yourself "oh it's just an 8 directional dash, how much can they really squeeze out of this?", and the answer is a lot.

As per usual with these kinds of games, it introduces new mechanics in every level, and then progressively builds more and more around them. Additionally, each new mechanic is kept rather simple: bubbles that give a short burst of speed and replenish jumps, moving platforms, an unspeakable lovecraftian void that you can dash through, you know, standard stuff. The result of this is that the new elements don't ever make the gameplay feel bloated, they just become elegant additions to the solid foundation that was already there. One aspect that is particularly unique is its amazing integration of momentum to the platforming, a lot of the moving platforms can give you speed in the direction that they travel as you hop off of them, which is often used in jumps and is a fantastic touch.

Another thing to note is Celeste doesn't shy away from making jumps difficult, yet perfectly calculated in such a way that it becomes incredibly satisfying at a mechanical level, while not simply being technical skill check, as a lot of the jumps do require some brains to figure out how to do properly. Consequently, the game feels quite fair, regardless of how long it takes to get a hard jump down, since you actually make steady progress with each attempt until the point of mastering it.

Not much needs to be said about the artstyle or OST I believe, they're excellent, and the remixes definitely keep you hyped up while tackling the B-sides (I haven't tried the C-sides yet, I'm missing some collectibles, please pray for me). The story is also nice, with endearing characters and an important lesson on self improvement and learning how to deal with the rough points in our lives which, let's face it, we've all been through. The use of climbing a mountain as a metaphor for this also justifies the game's difficulty, while bringing it all together in a very compelling way.

Beyond the fact that it's a bit short (which is fine anyway since there's a lot of extra levels and collectibles to keep you challenged), it's honestly a flawless game. It does everything right, and it's the most fun I've had with a platformer in a while. Also, it turned me into a woman, which I wasn't expecting but it seems to be a common side effect, I suppose. Eh, ♥♥♥♥ it, 10/10.

[h1]Peak skill-based platformer[/h1]

Matt first appeared on my radar around 2010 after playing his MoneySieze flash game on Kongregate. At a time I was neck deep in all kinds of indie and flash games, owning mostly to disappointment in modern games I had practically given up on. Amidst all that passed through, MS left such a huge impression it got me interested in author's other work, something that never happened before. Digging through [url=http://www.mattmakesgames.com/]Matt's website[/url] uncovered a treasure trove of high quality games, majority of which share Celeste genre (highly recommend Jumper series). Personal favorite and my 4th best game of all time is "An Untitled Story", a masterpiece metroidvania. One cannot go wrong with the site, all games are free. Mentioning it because Celeste has a [u]lot[/u] in common with MoneySieze and I figured many of you will appreciate checking the list although most if not all require Flash emulator nowadays.

Celeste here isn't your typical frustration or trial and error ridden platformer. That much you figured out by now from seeing the review score. Difficulty curve is present but sloped delicately to avoid sudden spikes and cheap gotcha moments, at least as far as main story Chapters 1-7 are concerned. I'd say it's a culmination of all of Matt's previous work with numerous carefully woven elements to create something gaming world has not seen before.

Gameplay is split into 9 Chapters with own visual style and unique gameplay mechanics tweaks that affect your approach to solving rooms. Every Chapter consists of roughly 30 such rooms and what you see is what you get, no hidden BS, any mistake you make shall be your own. Every room has a soft checkpoint and death respawn is near instant.
There are many safe places where our story unfolds, serving as main driving force pushing you forward. You lead a young girl, aged around high school years, discovering herself on her trek up the Celeste mountain while dealing with issues a person her age is expected to have. Writing is decent and delivered via skippable cutscenes and dialogues with several recurring NPCs encountered on the climb.

Now what would a platformer be without its most important parts: movement, abilities and obstacle course design. There is no human on Earth that does it better than Matt. Every jump, every maneuver will put you in absolute control at all times due confidence in precise yet error tolerant system under the hood. It'll make highly specific timings feel natural simply because of an absolute psycho-level dedication to code the cleanest of control schemes ever put in binary. I'm not exaggerating, movement code ended posted on his Twitter because the interest was so high. But like any other system it has its limits.
Abilities consist of jump, wall grab (free up/down climb but consumes stamina) and short 8-directional air dash that replenishes on contact with ground. The 3 basic abilities are greatly expanded by chapter specific mechanics and continuously evolving platforming puzzles so they never get old. If you think of yourself as a seasoned veteran believing you have seen it all before... think again. Not even mentioning many advanced techniques that are revealed throughout the course of gameplay that shine a new light on beginner courses you completed a week(s) ago.
Goal of every room, sized one or more screens, is simply to reach the end and enter the next one. Standing in your way are various insta-death hazards (bottom of screen, spikes, enemies, etc.) but arranged in a fair way so the majority are able to complete the main story. One of the hallmark of Matt's design principles since the early times is the easiest path is the fastest, meaning game rewards skill and you will gather plenty of it during the course. Even though I recently pushed 40 and still view myself above average it took 300 deaths per chapter while also getting collectibles and exploring harder hidden rooms present in all chapters. You are hereby witness this text testifying both to sturdiness of my Korean plastic keyboard makers and tolerance to high death counts the game miraculously provides.

Speaking of secrets there are plenty hidden passages behind breakable or fake walls and collectibles off the beaten path, all with in-game track records and various stats to marvel, as is case in most of his games. Master of sweetening the deal while holding a carrot in front of your face. Never before have players lived so hard to cheat death and fail. There's even a bonus 8-bit version hidden somewhere.

Music and sounds are fantastic, fitting the whole atmosphere thingy nicely. If you last to as early as Chapter 2 you will understand. Music also plays a pivotal role in certain hidden collectable rooms and it just shows how much effort and they put into audio stuff.

* * *

For all that is majestic there are parts I disliked. Difficulty and length of late-game courses become so devilish that it becomes far less skill related and turns to memorization instead. Execution of chains upon chains of pixel-perfect mini-second movements, jumps, dashes (and all kinds of rarely before used combinations) without moments rest. All kinds of wrongs that make up difficulty. I totally understand why though, with an amazing base to work with - why not take it to the extreme? And taken there it surely is. If I were still in my teens perhaps I'd think differently.
But fret not my elder gaming colleges for there are two saving graces to save the day: it's optional post-story content; and in-game "Assist Mode" readily available at all times. Devil resides only in Chapter 9 and C-sides. I held my ground up until Ch3 C-side, and for 1/3rd of Ch9 before resorting to Infinite Dash and Invulnerability. Body couldn't take it anymore, not to mention plastic Korean drowning on my sweat drops.
Great thing about Assist is that using it does not 'taint' your stats nor Steam achievements. Clear indication the whole dev team fully understands not to get in a way of battle-scared completionists! As much as I was frustrated with late-game content this one bone they offered made up for all of that.

Bit more persistent annoyance were 3 basic abilities and how hard it was to get used to them. In fact I never reached full consistency in execution and miss-presses were my most dominant cause of death until the end. Somehow I feel we have 1 ability too many that should have been fused with regular control method. Like removing wall grab in favor of auto grab when pushing against a wall or something, or combining dash with jump, and design levels around that. 3 just felt bit too much too often. Maybe my muscle memory is starting to degrade.

End of some chapters feature a Boss battle, essentially tightly timed chases that feel hugely out of place from regular gameplay. If anyone recalls, kinda like Boss battles in original Deux Ex: HR before they redesigned them to accommodate stealthy approach. They deepen the characters but lessen the gameplay.

Chapter checkpoint system does not offer enough starting points in order to go back and collect secrets you missed so a repeat of 10 minutes worth of platforming is required in worst cases. Although I get putting a loading point right beside a secret passage is not ideal it's better than needlessly wasting time. Induces fear of missing a secret and preemptive guide lookup to avoid that.

As decently as story is laid out the protagonist comes off as bit of a needy snowflake from the get go. Situation that was once successfully cured with 2 slaps if treatment started early. Feels forced and drags on for longer than it should have for my taste.

* * *

Most importantly Celeste is one in a lifetime platformer masterpiece. There will never be another unless same devs decide to create a sequel (kinda like La-Mulana). It simply requires knowledge no one else currently possesses. You owe it to yourself to experience it no matter your skill level or confidence.

Celeste is one of the best platformers ever made, hands down. The game asks a lot of the player in terms of precise platforming and timing, but it is ALWAYS rooting for you. Celeste wants you to win, and it's part of why it feels so good to play. The game "cheats" in favor of the player in a variety of ways - if you're a pixel off of a jump, the game gives you the landing anyway. Enemies universally have slightly smaller hitboxes than their graphics appear. There's other ways it fudges things slightly in your favor, but when you put it all together, you get a game that is still extremely hard, but every time you die, you know you deserved to take that death, because any time a situation is remotely questionable, the game is built to favor the player. It's an exquisite example of how to make a game extremely hard, but also have that difficulty consistently feel fair. I have thousands and thousands of deaths in this game and I think I can count on one hand how many times I've felt at all 'robbed.'

Game gud

Celeste is an example of a game developed with the utmost care and attention. It's my favorite platformer ever, and I really can't express how cleverly the mechanics, gameplay, and history fit all together in one well-wrapped game. Although some might consider the game a bit too harsh, remember that the devs made Celeste accessible to every skill level, whether you're new to platformers or a seasoned expert. This was the first game that didn't scare me when Speedrun or Kaizo levels were the subjects, because the game invites you every step of the way to learn new and hard stuff, and even the hidden mechanics are approachable for beginners while remaining hard to master. Spending time trying to get better and better truly made me love the game 100x more. Try pushing the game to its maximum, and you will be rewarded with nothing but satisfaction.

Psst! Want to know a secret? Try getting into modded Celeste; it has tons of community-created content. Celeste is my favorite game of all time.

When it comes to games, I'm somewhat of a masochist and completionist, and get bored easily when playing something not targeted for difficulty, except for certain games.  So, when I picked up Celeste out of a small amount of interest from Youtube and reviews, I thought I would probably enjoy it.

I was right, but not in the way I thought.  Sure, Celeste was also the hardest game I've ever played, and blah blah I've played Dark Souls blah blah Bloodborne and Hollow Knight blah blah etc.  But that's not why I enjoyed the experience so wholeheartedly.  I enjoyed Celeste because the game isn't all about difficulty like other titles.  The main difficulty of the game, in truth, is all optional.  The game is meant to be played to the Summit level, and the parts which are more difficult and rage inducing are meant to be optional.

I went through every part to completion, accumulating more than 30,000 deaths, and I can say with confidence that my enjoyment of the experience would have been the same had I stopped at the Summit.  But nonetheless I don't regret sinking my own time into it, and that is precisely what makes the game special; the individual experience you get from playing it to the end.  By the end, I mean when you choose to end YOUR playthrough.  What makes the difficulty of Celeste different and enjoyable is that the game doesn't give you any reason to believe that you are missing out by not pushing further into the game; the game lets you pick the difficulty you end it with, when you want to.  Whether you get to the Summit, Farewell, the Farewell Golden Berry, or whenever, as long as you can enjoy a somewhat difficult 2-D platformer, you will get a very large amount of enjoyment out of the game.

Still the level of enjoyment depends on the player.  Does raging at a difficult game ruin your entire day?  Don't play Celeste, and that's absolutely fine.  But if you can find even a small amount of enjoyment in difficulty, I recommend Celeste with my entire heart and soul, even if you only play past a few chapters.

Because, really, it doesn't matter who you are.  Celeste is tailored to you, not the other way around.

I think a quote from one of the chapters truly illustrates the way I felt after completing all of the content the game had to offer:

[spoiler] [i] "It's hard to believe that it's over, isn't it? Funny how we get attached to the struggle." [/i] [/spoiler]

Despite all of the times I became upset throughout, it was a sickeningly bittersweet realization that it was done; no more levels to work through and learn and master. Nothing but the highest recommendation for such an engaging work by the developers of Celeste.

One thing needs to be made clear first: this is a difficult game. If you expect some casual platforming while trying to relax after a hard day's work, this game is not for you. You will be expected to do tricky and precise moves right from the start and then it gets harder from there. But if you do spend the time and effort to keep up with the difficulty, you will be rewarded with awesome music and a nice story. I personally feel more touched by the story than I would have been just by reading it because I [i]struggled[/i] with our heroine and the conclusion of the story was a reward for that struggle. You wouldn't get the same feeling with an easy game.

If you want more after finishing the story, you'll have a lot of extra content to play through. You may not think you'll want to play that extra content while struggling with the main story; I didn't, either. But after a while, I realized I needed more Celeste in my life and started playing those extra-hard bonus levels. You may end up feeling the same if you give this game a chance!
